title: The 3-3-3 rule for clothes: 9 pieces, up to 27 outfits
h1: The 3-3-3 rule for clothes: how nine pieces make up to 27 outfits
excerpt: The 3-3-3 rule for clothes: three tops, three bottoms, three pairs of shoes. The honest outfit maths, a worked example and how it differs from Project 333.
tldr: The 3-3-3 rule means dressing from nine pieces: three tops, three bottoms and three pairs of shoes. If everything goes together that's 27 outfits; clashes lower the number and layering raises it. It's a short challenge or packing method, and it is not Project 333, which is 33 items for three months.
body:
The 3-3-3 rule for clothes means building every outfit from nine pieces: three tops, three bottoms and three pairs of shoes. If every piece goes with every other, that's 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 outfits. People use it for a trip, a week or a style reset rather than as a permanent wardrobe size.

It is a different thing from Project 333, which is 33 items for three months. More on that below.

What the 3-3-3 rule for clothes means

You pick nine pieces and wear only those, combining them in as many ways as you can. The limit is the point: with so few options, you find pairings you'd never have tried with a full wardrobe.

The version that spread online came from TikTok. Refinery29 credits creator Rachel Spencer with coining the "333 method" of three tops, three bottoms and three pairs of shoes; in one of her videos she made 19 different outfits from her nine pieces.

There is no official rulebook, so details vary. Some versions swap the shoes for three layers, such as a blazer, a cardigan and a jacket. Most leave out underwear, socks, sleepwear and gym clothes. Coats and accessories are where versions disagree, so decide before you start and stick to it.

The 3-3-3 rule vs Project 333

Search results often blur the two, and the names don't help. Here is the difference:

3-3-3 ruleProject 333
Size9 pieces: 3 tops, 3 bottoms, 3 pairs of shoes33 items
What countsMain garments and shoes; accessories usually don'tClothes, shoes, accessories, jewellery and outerwear
How longNo set length: a trip, a week, a month-long challengeThree months, then you choose again
The rest of your clothesNo formal ruleBoxed up and put out of sight
OriginPopularised on TikTokCourtney Carver, 2010

In short, the 3-3-3 rule is a styling exercise and Project 333 is a whole-wardrobe challenge. If the 33-item version is the one you're after, our guide to Project 333 rules and what counts covers it in full.

The outfit maths, honestly

The 27 comes from multiplying the choices: any of 3 tops, with any of 3 bottoms, with any of 3 pairs of shoes. That number assumes two things, and both bend in real life.

Clashes bring it down. Every top-and-bottom or shoe-and-bottom pairing that doesn't work removes three outfits, one for each of the other category's pieces. Two bad pairings and you're at 21.

Layering pushes it up. The maths treats each outfit as one top. But a jumper over a collared shirt, or a shirt worn open over a T-shirt, is a different look from either piece on its own. Each layered combination that works adds a new "top" to the multiplication.

So 27 is neither a promise nor a ceiling. It's a starting estimate that depends on how well the nine pieces were chosen.

A worked example that works for anyone

These nine pieces are deliberately plain so the example works whatever your style or body. Swap any of them for your own equivalent.

TopsBottomsShoes
White T-shirtDark straight-leg jeansWhite leather trainers
Light-blue oxford shirtBlack tailored trousersBrown leather boots
Navy crew-neck jumperBeige chinosBlack loafers

Now the count, step by step:

StepSumOutfits
On paper, everything goes with everything3 × 3 × 327
Say you don't like brown boots with black trousers: 8 of the 9 shoe-and-bottom pairings work3 tops × 824
Add two layered tops: the jumper over the oxford shirt, and the shirt worn open over the T-shirt5 tops × 840

Forty is the theoretical count. You won't wear all of them, and you don't need to. A few that show the range:

  • Saturday errands: jeans, white T-shirt, white trainers.
  • Office day: black trousers, oxford shirt, loafers.
  • Cold evening out: jeans, jumper over the oxford shirt, brown boots.
  • Warm afternoon: chinos, shirt open over the T-shirt, trainers.
  • Smart-casual dinner: black trousers, navy jumper, loafers.

To adapt it, swap the chinos for a midi skirt, the boots for heeled ankle boots, or the oxford for a silk blouse; the maths stays the same. A dress or jumpsuit fills a bottom slot but can't be paired with tops, so it adds fewer combinations, mainly with shoes and layers.

How to choose your nine pieces

  1. Stick to one colour family. Two neutrals and one accent colour is the easy version. If you want a pattern, limit it to one piece.
  2. Spread the formality. In each category, aim for one casual piece, one in-between and one smart. That's what lets the same nine cover a Saturday and a meeting.
  3. Pick shoes for your week, not your wishlist. One pair for walking, one for weather, one that dresses things up. Shoes usually decide whether an outfit works.
  4. Include one top that layers. A shirt you can wear open, or a jumper that fits over a collar, is the cheapest way to add outfits.
  5. Test every pairing before you commit. Lay the nine pieces out on a bed and check all nine top-and-bottom pairings and all nine shoe-and-bottom pairings. Swap out anything that only works with one other piece.

Laying them out on a bed does the job. FitWardrobe is our app, and it isn't available yet; when it opens, you'll be able to photograph your pieces and ask for an outfit built around one of them, which is another quick way to test a nine-piece set.

Using the 3-3-3 rule for a trip

For a long weekend or a short work trip, nine pieces plus underwear, socks and sleepwear fit easily in a carry-on. Wear the bulkiest shoes and your jacket while travelling so they don't take up space in the bag. If a coat or swimwear is essential where you're going, add it on top and don't agonise over the count.

For a week or longer, a slightly bigger formula is easier to live with. The 5-4-3-2-1 method counts down from five tops and four bottoms to a single extra; versions differ on what fills the last slots. Our capsule packing guide walks through it with examples.

Where the rule falls short

  • Cold or wet weather. Nine pieces with no coat only works in a mild climate or indoors. In winter, treat outerwear as outside the count or the challenge stops being practical.
  • Laundry. Three tops in hot weather means washing every couple of days.
  • Varied weeks. A wedding, a gym habit or a job with a dress code needs clothes the nine won't cover. Treat those as separate from the challenge.
  • Long-term use. Dressing from nine pieces for months is hard to sustain. For a small wardrobe you can keep all year, a capsule wardrobe of a few dozen pieces is the more realistic version of the same idea.

If you'd like the nine pieces to last a whole week without repeating a full outfit, plan the days ahead using our guide to planning seven outfits for the week. Seven different combinations from nine pieces is comfortably within reach.

faq.q: What is the 3-3-3 rule capsule wardrobe?
faq.a: It's a nine-piece mini capsule: three tops, three bottoms and three pairs of shoes that all work together. You wear only those pieces for a set period, such as a trip or a week, and combine them in as many ways as possible. If every piece pairs with every other, that's 27 outfits. Underwear, socks, sleepwear and gym clothes don't count.

faq.q: How many outfits does the 3-3-3 rule make?
faq.a: On paper, 27: three tops times three bottoms times three pairs of shoes. In practice the number moves both ways. Pairings that clash remove three outfits each, and layering one top over another adds new combinations. TikTok creator Rachel Spencer made 19 outfits from her nine pieces in one video, which is a realistic target for a well-chosen set.

faq.q: Is the 3-3-3 rule the same as Project 333?
faq.a: No. The 3-3-3 rule is nine pieces: three tops, three bottoms and three pairs of shoes, usually for a short challenge or a trip. Project 333 is Courtney Carver's challenge of wearing 33 items, including accessories, jewellery and outerwear, for three months while the rest of your clothes are boxed up. The similar names cause most of the confusion.

faq.q: What is the 3-3-3 rule for packing for a trip?
faq.a: Pack three tops, three bottoms and three pairs of shoes that all mix together, then add underwear, socks, sleepwear and anything the destination demands, such as a coat or swimwear. Wear the heaviest shoes and jacket while travelling. Nine coordinated pieces cover a long weekend or a short work trip comfortably and usually fit in a carry-on bag.

faq.q: What is the 5 4 3 2 1 method of wardrobe?
faq.a: It's a packing countdown for longer trips: five tops, four bottoms, three of the next category, two of the one after and one final extra. Versions differ on the last three slots, which may be shoes, layers, dresses, swimwear or an accessory. It gives more variety than the 3-3-3 rule, so it suits a week or more away.

faq.q: Does the 3-3-3 rule work for men?
faq.a: Yes. The rule is the same for everyone because it only counts tops, bottoms and shoes. A typical set might be a white T-shirt, an oxford shirt and a navy jumper; dark jeans, chinos and smart trousers; and white trainers, leather boots and loafers. Keep the colours close and include one top that layers over another.
